name: Exploiting vulnerabilities for which a patch exists (attacking non-updated software)
description: These are known vulnerabilities that have been reported and have working patches (updates which fix the vulnerability), but some systems remain unpatched because of lax update policies or because of the use of products for which patches are no longer being provided by the vendor.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Exploiting reported but not (fully) patched vulnerabilities
description: These are known vulnerabilities for which the vendor has either not provided a patch or provided a patch that only partially addressed the issue, primarily because of the challenge of patching the vulnerabilities comprehensively.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Finding and exploiting individual zero-days
description: Zero-days are vulnerabilities that are not yet identified by the vendor or the broader cybersecurity commu- nity.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Direct access to zero-days at scale
description: Capable state actors are also likely to have (official or surreptitious) access to information on not yet publicly disclosed zero-days for which a patch has not been officially released.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Social engineering
description: A relatively cheap and nonrisky toolset for influencing employees to perform actions that would allow an attack.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Password brute-forcing and cracking
description: Attackers masquerade as a user(s) with permissions thanks to password brute-forcing and cracking.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Exploitation of exposed credentials
description: Authorized users may be careless with their credentials and leave them accessible to an attacker.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Expanding illegitimate access (e.g., escalating privileges)
description: Existing credentials are often obtained by first gaining some illegitimate access to a system (e.g., using other tools described in this report) and then obtaining credentials that provide further access.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

category: Undermining the Access Control System Itself
name: Encryption/authentication vulnerabilities (in the access control system)
description: This vector entails breaking the existing encryption/authentication scheme underlying the security of the access control system.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

category: Undermining the Access Control System Itself
name: Intentional backdoors in algorithms, protocols, or products (in the access control system)
description: Backdoor is a term for flaws intentionally introduced into a security-related algorithm or protocol, rendering it insecure (either to anyone who identifies this flaw or only to those who have access to some backdoor key or secret).
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

category: Undermining the Access Control System Itself
name: Code vulnerabilities (in the access control system)
description: Most access control systems are either software systems or have significant software components.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

category: Undermining the Access Control System Itself
name: Access to secret material undermining a protocol
description: An attacker can gain illegitimate access to a key or other secret that undermines the reliability of a protocol or platform—even if that secret does not belong to the victim.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Incorrect configuration or security policy implementation
description: Configuration errors may unintentionally enable access.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Additional (less secure) copies of sensitive data
description: Additional copies of the weights (or other sensitive materials) may not be monitored or secured as thoroughly as the “main copy.” The copy might be intentionally created (e.g., backup copies or local copies used by research teams), but the security team is unaware of its existence or has not invested in adequately securing it.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Alternative (less secure) authentication or access schemes
description: Many systems have nonstandard authentication or access pathways.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Discovering existing vulnerabilities in the ML stack
description: Adversaries may exploit preexisting vulnerabilities in the ML software and hardware stack (including the full supply chain) to execute malicious code or otherwise undermine the security of the models or the broader system.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Intentional ML supply chain compromise
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Prompt-triggered code execution
description: This consists of bypassing restrictions of a model that is able to execute code by specially crafting prompts to manipulate the model’s behavior (known as prompt injection).
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Model extraction
description: The answer to each query of the model bears information on the weights that helped produce it.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Model distillation
description: Adversaries can replicate the functionality of a private ML model by making repeated queries to its inference API.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

category: Nontrivial Access to Data or Networks
name: Digital access to air-gapped networks
description: Penetrating and exfiltrating information from a system that is not ethernet-connected but that has lots of communications (e.g., via USB sticks) is more challenging than doing so for a fully internet-connected system, but it still has significant precedent.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

category: Nontrivial Access to Data or Networks
name: Side-channel attacks (including through leaked emanations; i.e., TEMPEST attacks)
description: Electronic information can often be detected or inferred using various leaking emanations, including conducted electromagnetic emissions (e.g., electricity usage), optical emissions, acoustic sounds, radiated electromagnetic emissions, radio signals, caches (especially across cloud instances), and differential fault analysis.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

category: Nontrivial Access to Data or Networks
name: Eavesdropping and wiretaps
description: An attacker can take other actions to collect sensitive information in a continuous manner, including sending individuals to physically listen to conversations (with or without the assistance of specialized devices); plant- ing microphones, cameras, or other automated devices; tapping wires (phone lines, ethernet cables, inter- net backbone, etc.) to covertly access communicated data; and other approaches.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Direct physical access to sensitive systems
description: If no exceptional security practices are in place, an attacker can often directly access physical servers (or other devices).
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Malicious placement of portable devices
description: A common and easy-to-execute strategy is to leave devices (most commonly USB flash drives, but also hard drives, computer peripherals, and other devices) laying around the target facility (in the office, in the parking lot, in the elevator).
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Physical access to devices in other locations
description: If the premises are well secured, attackers could try to access organization devices in other locations.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Evasion of physical access control systems
description: Many physical security systems critically rely on digital systems (e.g., cameras, alert systems, digital locks).
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Penetration of physical hardware security
description: In high-security contexts, some devices will have physical hardware protections (e.g., HSMs, smartcards, and other secure cryptoprocessors—see more details in Appendix B).
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Armed break-in
description: This vector is a variation on direct physical access, but with much more capable agents who are both better trained in gaining access and have a broader toolset at their disposal—including drugging security personnel and using violence if necessary.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Military takeover
description: At the extreme end of physical attacks, an attacker might use military force to take over a facility.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Services and equipment the organization uses
description: This includes computers, paraphernalia, GPUs and ML-specific hardware, electric wiring in the walls, USB devices that might be connected, security keys, printers and office equipment, chip-embedded code (e.g., Intel’s AMT vulnerability, Silent Bob Is Silent),179 operating systems, code repositories, Continuous Integra- tion and Continuous Deployment infrastructure, compiled artifact repositories, developer sandboxes, and staging systems, monitoring and instrumentation, and other proximate systems that are directly involved in building and maintaining research or deployed production models, ML
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Code and infrastructure incorporated into the codebase
description: Some code and infrastructure are not developed by the organization; they are developed by third parties and then incorporated into the organization’s codebase.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Vendors with access to information
description: A separate attack vector is vendors who have access to sensitive data or systems; if the vendors are compro- mised (even on a completely separate network), an organization’s data can be compromised.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Bribes and cooperation
description: People can be paid or persuaded to take actions on behalf of an adversary.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Extortion
description: Instead of providing benefits, an adversary can threaten a person with physical harm, legal harm, financial harm, and more.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Candidate placement
description: In a more sophisticated variation, capable adversaries may employ and train people before they join the orga- nization and help them become strong candidates for sensitive roles.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Organizational leverage attacks
description: At the more strategic or institutional level, the organization itself can be coerced or fooled into playing into the adversary’s hand.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A

name: Organizationally approved access
description: Like organizational leverage attacks, these attacks can be implemented with the known cooperation of some or all of the executive leaders of the organization.
source: Nevo et al. 2024, RAND RR-A2849-1, Table 5.1 (p. 12) / Appendix A
